hints: Think about what must stay exactly the same for two compounds to be isomers, count the atoms of each element.
Think about what must be different, focus on the order atoms are joined together, not just their shape in space.
walkthrough:
Fix what is identical**
Picture $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}$. Any structural isomer of this must also contain exactly 3 carbons, 6 hydrogens and 1 oxygen. Isomers always share the same molecular formula, so the atom count never changes.

Pin down what is different**
What changes is how those atoms are linked. One isomer might have a $\text{C=O}$ group, another might have a $\text{C=C}$ plus a $\text{C-O}$ group. Different connectivity means different displayed or structural formulae, even though the molecular formula is identical.

Final answer: Compounds with the same molecular formula, same number of atoms of each element.
With different structural formulae, different arrangement of atoms and bonds.

hints: Start from carbon's valence orbitals, one 2s and three 2p orbitals, and remember hybridisation is mixing of these atomic orbitals.
Count how many p orbitals mix with the s orbital in each case, two p for one type and three p for the other.
walkthrough:
Recall the starting orbitals**
Carbon uses its second shell for bonding, one $2s$ orbital and three $2p$ orbitals. Hybridisation is simply the mathematical mixing of these atomic orbitals on the same carbon to make a new set of equal energy hybrid orbitals for sigma bonding.

Separate the two cases**
For $sp^2$, you mix the $2s$ with only two of the $2p$ orbitals, leaving one $p$ orbital unhybridised to form a pi bond. That gives three $sp^2$ orbitals in a plane. For $sp^3$, you mix the $2s$ with all three $2p$ orbitals, giving four identical $sp^3$ orbitals pointing tetrahedrally, with no p orbital left over.

Final answer: $sp^2$ hybridisation: overlap / mixing of (2)s orbital with two (2)p orbitals.
$sp^3$ hybridisation: overlap / mixing of (2)s orbital with all three (2)p orbitals.

hints: Picture the shape made by three regions of electron density around carbon, as in an alkene or carbonyl.
Picture the shape made by four regions of electron density around carbon, as in an alkane or alcohol.
walkthrough:
Link $sp^2$ to trigonal planar**
Three $sp^2$ orbitals repel each other equally in a plane. Three equal repulsions fit perfectly at $120^{\circ}$ apart. So any $\text{C=C}$ or $\text{C=O}$ carbon is essentially flat with about $120^{\circ}$ angles.

Link $sp^3$ to tetrahedral**
Four $sp^3$ orbitals repel equally in three dimensions. The most spread out arrangement is tetrahedral, with an angle of $109.5^{\circ}$. That is the normal angle around a saturated carbon with four single bonds.

Final answer: $sp^2$: $120^{\circ}$ (accept $116^{\circ}$ to $124^{\circ}$).
$sp^3$: $109.5^{\circ}$ (accept $106^{\circ}$ to $112^{\circ}$).

hints: Cold dilute acidified manganate(VII) adds two OH groups across the C=C bond, so work backwards by removing two OH groups from propane-1,2,3-triol to leave one C=C.
walkthrough:
Work backwards from the triol**
Cold, dilute $\text{MnO}_4^-$ does mild oxidation, it adds an $\text{-OH}$ to each carbon of the $\text{C=C}$. Your product has $\text{OH}$ on all three carbons: $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{OH}$. To get back to $\mathbf{R}$, remove the middle $\text{OH}$ and one end $\text{OH}$ and join those two carbons with a double bond.

Draw $\mathbf{R}$ fully displayed**
That leaves one $\text{-OH}$ untouched plus a new $\text{C=C}$. So $\mathbf{R}$ is prop-2-en-1-ol: $\text{HO-CH}_2\text{-CH=CH}_2$. In a displayed formula show every bond: $\text{H-O-C}$ with two H on the first C, one H on the middle C, and two H on the end C with a double bond between the last two carbons.
Final answer: Displayed formula of $\mathbf{R}$ is $\text{HO-CH}_2\text{-CH=CH}_2$ with all bonds and all H atoms shown.

hints: Recall the general mechanism type when $\text{Br}_2$ attacks the electron rich C=C double bond.
Recall the colour of aqueous bromine before reaction and what happens to that colour when the $\text{Br-Br}$ is consumed.
walkthrough:
Name the reaction type**
The $\text{C=C}$ in $\mathbf{R}$ is electron rich and attracts electrophiles. $\text{Br}_2$ adds across the double bond, both Br atoms ending up on the molecule. That is electrophilic addition, characteristic of all alkenes.

Describe the observation**
Bromine water is orange brown. When it adds to the alkene it is used up to make a colourless dibromo compound, so the solution turns from orange brown to colourless. That colour loss is the positive test for unsaturation.

Final answer: Electrophilic addition.
Orange / brown bromine water is decolourised to colourless.

hints: Add one Br atom to each carbon of the original C=C in R, keeping the alcohol group unchanged.
walkthrough:
Add Br across the double bond**
Start with $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH=CH}_2$. Break the pi bond and attach a Br to the middle carbon and a Br to the end carbon. The $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$ end is untouched. You get $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{Br}$, which is 2,3-dibromopropan-1-ol.
Final answer: $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{Br}$ shown as displayed or structural formula.

hints: Hot concentrated acidified manganate(VII) breaks C-C bonds completely, oxidising carbon chains fully to the highest oxidation state gas.
walkthrough:
Recognise strong oxidation**
Hot, concentrated $\text{MnO}_4^-$ does not stop at the diol, it cleaves the molecule aggressively. Organic material containing C, H and O is oxidised right up to $\text{CO}_2$ plus water. The gaseous product that bubbles off is carbon dioxide, $\text{CO}_2$.
Final answer: $\text{CO}_2$, carbon dioxide.

hints: Both P and Q give an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH, so decide what functional group both must contain given formula $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}$.
Only Q gives a yellow precipitate with alkaline aqueous iodine, so recall which carbonyl arrangement, ethanal or methyl ketone, gives the iodoform reaction.
walkthrough:
Use 2,4-DNPH to find the family**
An orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH means a carbonyl compound, an aldehyde or a ketone. With $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}$ there are only two possibilities: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$. Both have O bonded to an $sp^2$ carbon, matching the stem.

Use iodine to split them**
Alkaline aqueous iodine gives a yellow precipitate only with a $\text{CH}_3\text{CO-}$ group. Propanone $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$ has this group, propanal $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$ does not. So the positive one, $\mathbf{Q}$, must be propanone, leaving $\mathbf{P}$ as propanal.

Final answer: $\mathbf{P}$ = propanal, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$.
$\mathbf{Q}$ = propanone, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$.

hints: Remember the name and formula of the pale yellow solid with an antiseptic smell formed in the iodoform test.
walkthrough:
Name the yellow solid**
The iodoform reaction converts the $\text{CH}_3\text{CO-}$ group into a yellow precipitate of triiodomethane, $\text{CHI}_3$, sometimes written as iodoform. That is the solid you filter off.
Final answer: Triiodomethane, $\text{CHI}_3$.

hints: Think about what stays the same for optical isomers, both the molecular formula and the connectivity.
Think about what makes them different, focus on 3D arrangement, mirror images, and a carbon with four different groups.
walkthrough:
Fix the sameness**
Optical isomers are not structural isomers. They have identical connectivity, the same structural formula. The difference is purely in space.

Describe the 3D difference**
They exist as a pair of mirror images that cannot be laid exactly on top of each other, just like left and right hands. This happens when a carbon is attached to four different atoms or groups, a chiral centre. The two forms rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions.

Final answer: Molecules with the same molecular and structural formula.
That are non-superimposable mirror images of each other / have a chiral centre with four different groups attached / differ in 3D spatial arrangement / rotate plane-polarised light differently.

hints: Identify the nucleophile, the lone pair on $:\text{C}\equiv\text{N}^-$, and the electrophile, the $\delta+$ carbon of $\text{C=O}$, and show the first curly arrow.
Show the polarity of the carbonyl $^{\delta+}\text{C}=\text{O}^{\delta-}$ and the second curly arrow from the C=O bond onto oxygen.
Think about the intermediate formed, a $\text{C-O}^-$ alkoxide, and how it is protonated by HCN or $\text{H}^+$ to give $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CN}$.
walkthrough:
Set up the polar carbonyl**
Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so draw $\text{CH}_3\text{-C}^{\delta+}\text{(H)=O}^{\delta-}$. The carbon is electron poor and open to attack. The real nucleophile is $:\text{CN}^-$ from HCN with KCN catalyst. Draw a curly arrow from its lone pair straight to the $\text{C}^{\delta+}$.

Form the alkoxide intermediate**
As the new $\text{C-C}$ bond forms, the $\text{C=O}$ pi electrons must move. Draw a curly arrow from the $\text{C=O}$ double bond onto the oxygen, giving $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(O}^-\text{)CN}$. Check charges: N is neutral in the nitrile, O now carries $-$ .

Protonate to the cyanohydrin**
The $\text{O}^-$ is strongly basic. It takes $\text{H}^+$ from HCN (or from acid in a second step). Draw a curly arrow from the $\text{O}^-$ lone pair to $\text{H}^+$. This gives the final product $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CN}$ and regenerates $\text{CN}^-$.

Final answer: Nucleophilic addition mechanism: $^{\delta+}\text{C}=\text{O}^{\delta-}$ shown with curly arrow $\text{C=O}$ to $\text{O}$; curly arrow from $:\text{CN}^-$ lone pair to $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ to give $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(O}^-\text{)CN}$ intermediate; curly arrow from $\text{O}^-$ lone pair to $\text{H}^+$ / HCN to give $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CN}$.
